sections.html:
• Scientific name: Brachyplatystoma vaillantii (Valenciennes, 1840)
  • Size: 1500 mm (59.1 in) SL
  • Temperature: 24.0–27.0°C
  • pH: 6.0–7.6
  • Identification: gray dorsal surface and underside. The large adipose fin clearly separates it from other congeners.
  • Etymology: Greek brachys = short, platys = flat, stoma = mouth.
• IUCN Red List: Least Concern (IUCN 2024). Despite the little information available, the species has a wide range and no apparent threats that put it at risk of extinction.
South America: Amazon and Orinoco River basins and major rivers of the Guianas and northeastern Brazil. Type locality: Cayenne, French Guiana; Suriname; Colombia.
South America: Amazon and Orinoco River basins and major rivers of the Guianas and northeastern Brazil.
Naturally found in muddy, black water and clear waters as far downstream as freshwater estuary habitat.

In the Amazon, they congregate in schools at the Rio Madeira rapids every four to five years (Goulding 1981). These schools apparently originate in the Amazon estuaries and migrate upstream as far as the Rio Solimoes. It can sometimes be caught in the upper part up to the foot of the Andean range, where it appears to be more rare than Brachyplatystoma filamentosum, but never in the zones prone to flood. Reproductive migrations probably occur like in other Brachyplatystoma. Usually caught with long lines and drift nets. Its flesh is of excellent quality and highly appreciated.
Breeding: unreported. There is no breeding report.

Resembles B. filamentosum, but B. vaillantii has a larger adipose fin and does not grow as large as the former.

Etymology: the specific name vaillantii honours François Levaillant (1753–1824), French explorer, naturalist and zoological collector, who brought the types to Europe.
Histoire naturelle des poissons v. 15, pp 21, Pl. 423.
